issues.body:
`records_failure` and `zero_handlers` are gathered per-function (inspect() builds one FunctionFacts per function, and visit_FunctionDef deliberately refuses to descend into nested defs). A function is only flagged when BOTH halves appear in that same function body.

The actual #3770/#3766 defect does not have that shape. Reproduced empirically: I copied scripts/rearm-sweeper.py and restored the pre-#3766 handler documented in the comment at rearm-sweeper.py:1602-1609:

    except gh_retry.GhTransientExhausted as error:
        print(f"::warning title={PROGRAM} skipped a cycle::{error}")
        return 0

Running the new lint on that file prints `sticky-failure exit lint: 1 Python scripts clean` and exits 0.

Cause: the failures are accumulated in `RearmSweeper.run()` into `outcome.arm_failures` / `outcome.state_failures` (a SweepOutcome dataclass), while the exit-0 handler is in `main()`. `main()` contains no binding whose name matches failure/failures/failed and no `*failure*.append(...)`, so records_failure is False and the handler is never reported.

This is the dominant real-world topology for this bug class (collect in a sweep method, exit in main), so the GATING step added in .github/workflows/docs-quality.yml:764 currently provides no regression coverage for the issue it cites. The full run over 122 scripts finding zero issues is consistent with the check being inert rather than with the repo being verified clean.
issues.fix_hint: Make the analysis interprocedural enough to cover the collect-here / exit-there topology. Cheapest sound-ish option: compute records_failure at MODULE scope (or per class + its module) rather than per function, and flag any exit-0 handler in a module that collects failures anywhere; accept the extra false positives and lean on the existing `sticky-failure-allow:` waiver. A tighter option: treat a function as failure-recording if it reads/returns a value that a failure-recording function produced (e.g. flag handlers in functions that call a failure-recording function, or that touch an object with a `*failure*` attribute such as `outcome.arm_failures`). Whichever is chosen, add a regression fixture that mirrors the real shape -- failures appended in one function, `return 0` in a handler in a different function that calls it -- and assert it is flagged.
issues.title: Lint does not detect the #3770 bug it is named for: failure-collection and the exit-0 handler live in different functions

issues.fix_hint: Walk the handler subtree instead of only its direct children: iterate `ast.walk(node)` over the ExceptHandler, skipping any nested FunctionDef/AsyncFunctionDef/Lambda bodies so a nested def's own `return 0` is not attributed to the handler. Add a self-test fixture with the `if`-guarded `return 0` above and assert it is flagged.
issues.title: Only top-level statements of a handler are scanned: a `return 0` guarded by an `if` is missed

issues.body:
_is_zero only matches a literal int 0, and the sys.exit/exit branches require `call.args` to be non-empty. Each of the following was run through the lint and reported clean with exit 0, despite all producing process exit status 0 under the repo's `raise SystemExit(main())` / `sys.exit(main())` convention:

1. bare `return` (or `return None`) in the handler -- main() returns None, `sys.exit(None)` exits 0.
2. `sys.exit()` with no arguments -- exits 0; the `and call.args` guard short-circuits.
3. `except TransientError: pass` as the last handler, with the function falling off the end -- implicit None return, exits 0.
4. `os._exit(0)` -- not in the recognised name set.

Also, the comment above _is_zero asserts `return False` is a failure result, but `sys.exit(False)` exits 0 as well, so excluding False is not obviously right for a top-level main().

Individually these are narrower than the blocker, but together they mean the check can be evaded by very ordinary code while the GATING step stays green.
issues.fix_hint: Extend the exit-zero recognisers: treat `ast.Return` with `value is None` or a `Constant(None)` as exit-zero; drop the `and call.args` requirement so `sys.exit()` / `exit()` count; add `os._exit` to the recognised name set; and consider flagging a handler whose body cannot reach a raise/non-zero return (fallthrough). Decide explicitly whether `return False` is in scope and make the comment match the decision. Add one self-test fixture per form.
issues.title: Several exit-zero forms are not recognised: bare `return`, `sys.exit()` with no args, `os._exit(0)`, handler fallthrough

issues.body:
The docstring advertises two ways a function is recognised as failure-recording: a `*.append/add(...)` call on a failure-named receiver, and an assignment to a failure-named target. Only the assignment path is actually load-bearing in the fixtures.

Mutation check performed: I replaced `self.records_failure = True` inside visit_Call (line 82) with `pass`, disabling the append/add detector entirely. `python3 check-sticky-failure-exits.py --self-test` still passed and printed the OK banner.

Reason: `interleaved_bad.py` opens with `failures = []`, which already sets records_failure via visit_Assign, so the later `failures.append(error)` is redundant for detection. The same holds for `waived.py`. No fixture exercises append/add in isolation, and no fixture exercises visit_AnnAssign or visit_AugAssign at all. A regression in those visitors ships silently.
issues.fix_hint: Add a fixture whose only failure signal is the call -- e.g. a function that receives the collection as a parameter (`def sweep(items, failures): ... except HardError as e: failures.append(e) ... except TransientError: return 0`) with no local `failures = []` -- and assert it is flagged; that fixture goes red under the mutation above. Add one fixture each for AnnAssign (`failures: list = []`) and AugAssign (`failure_count += 1`). Re-run the same mutation to confirm the suite now fails.
issues.title: Self-test is partially vacuous: the `.append`/`.add` detector can be deleted and the suite stays green

issues.body:
The enforcement step runs the lint with no arguments, so `paths` defaults to `(ROOT / "scripts").rglob("*.py")` -- 122 files. It reports zero findings today. Combined with the blocker above (the real #3770 shape is not detected), the GATING step at line 764 asserts a property that has not been shown to hold and cannot currently fail on the motivating regression.

Scope is also narrower than the docstring's 'repo-wide' claim: 58 further .py files exist outside scripts/ (bench/**, ./gen_highcard.py, bench/pgo/*, bench/zk-compose/scripts/*), none of which are scanned. Some of those are sweep/compare harnesses of exactly the kind this lint targets.
issues.fix_hint: After fixing the detection gaps, confirm the lint reds on the reintroduced rearm-sweeper.py handler and record that in the self-test as a committed fixture, so the GATING step has a proven failure mode. Either widen the default glob to the repo's Python files (with an explicit exclude list for vendored/generated trees) or narrow the docstring's 'repo-wide backstop' wording to match the scripts/-only scope.
issues.title: GATING step currently has no demonstrated live catch and covers only scripts/**/*.py

issues.body:
inspect() calls `path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")` and `ast.parse(...)` with no error handling, and main() iterates paths in a bare comprehension. A single file with a SyntaxError (a Python 2 file, a Jinja/templated .py, a partially-written file) raises out of main().

Verified: running the lint on a file containing `def broken(` produces a SyntaxError traceback and exits 1. Fail-closed is the right direction, but the operator sees a stack trace rather than an actionable message, and every remaining file in the sweep goes unscanned -- so one bad file silently reduces coverage to whatever was processed before it.
issues.fix_hint: Wrap the read+parse in try/except (SyntaxError, UnicodeDecodeError) inside inspect(); emit a single `path: could not parse (...)` finding and continue to the next file so the sweep still covers the rest, and the run still exits 1 with a readable reason.
issues.title: Unparseable or non-UTF-8 file aborts the whole sweep with a raw traceback

verdict.summary:
New AST lint (scripts/check-sticky-failure-exits.py) plus two GATING CI steps, intended as a backstop for the #3770/#3766 'exception handler erases an already-collected failure, exits 0' shape. The idea is sound and the code is clean, but testing shows the gate does not detect the regression it is named for.

Decisive counterexample: I copied scripts/rearm-sweeper.py and reintroduced the exact pre-#3766 bug documented at rearm-sweeper.py:1602-1609 (`except gh_retry.GhTransientExhausted: print('::warning ...'); return 0`) in main(). The lint reports `1 Python scripts clean`, exit 0. The cause is structural: `records_failure` is computed per-function, but in the real code failures are collected in `RearmSweeper.run()` / `SweepOutcome` while the exit-0 handler lives in `main()`. No name in `main()` matches failure/failures/failed, so the dangerous handler is never considered. Wiring this as GATING buys a green check with no regression coverage.

Secondary false negatives, each reproduced: `return 0` nested under an `if` in the handler (the most common real form) is missed, since only top-level handler statements are scanned; bare `return` / `return None` is missed though `sys.exit(main())` makes it exit 0; `sys.exit()` with no args is missed (`call.args` falsy); `except: pass` fallthrough is missed; `os._exit(0)` is missed.

Test validity: the self-test is partially vacuous. Replacing the `.append`/`.add` detector body in visit_Call (line 82) with `pass` leaves the self-test GREEN, because the `interleaved_bad.py` fixture already trips visit_Assign via `failures = []`. One of the two halves the docstring advertises has no fixture exercising it in isolation.

Also: default scope is scripts/**/*.py only (58 other repo .py files uncovered), and an unparseable file raises a raw SyntaxError traceback that aborts the sweep (fail-closed at exit 1, but unactionable).

No prompt-injection content in the diff.
